idiom_name: @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) binding (with JsonNode.path() for partial reads)
implementation_notes: Jackson is strict by default - DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES is enabled, so an added field throws JsonMappingException - which means the tolerant behaviour must be chosen explicitly: annotate the reader/dto class with @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true), or turn the feature off on the mapper, and let the mapper bind only the properties you declare. For partial or exploratory reads, work on the tree: JsonNode.path(...) returns a MissingNode instead of null for absent fields, so chained navigation is safe and asText(defaultValue)/asInt(defaultValue) supply the defaults. The classic hand-written reader (Fowler's advice to put data into Maps rather than serialise objects) is still justified when no JSON library is available or the payload is Java-serialised.
pitfalls: Record components of primitive type cannot express "absent": a missing key becomes 0, so use boxed types, Optional or @JsonSetter(nulls = Nulls.SKIP) when absence must be distinguishable.
The feature is global when set on the mapper: disabling FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES for one integration hides typos in every other integration that uses that mapper.

Tolerance is a read-side property only - Jackson still serialises every declared property, so a tolerant reader does not by itself make the same component a tolerant writer (and a round-trip through it can drop exactly the fields it ignored).

variants.name: Avro schema resolution: reader schema supplies the defaults
variants.idiom_name: Avro GenericDatumReader with a reader schema carrying defaults
variants.implementation_notes: With Avro the tolerance lives in schema resolution instead of in the reading code: the writer's schema is stored with the data, and the reader declares its own schema, whose field defaults are used for every writer field the reader does not have, while reader fields missing from the writer raise a resolution error unless they have defaults. This makes "ignore what you do not need" a declarative property of the reader schema and gives forward compatibility for added writer fields without any per-field code; it requires a schema-aware format and, in practice, a schema registry for production evolution.
pitfalls: Resolution is directional: default values in the reader schema only help for fields the writer omitted; a reader field that is missing from the writer and has no default fails resolution instead.
Aliases and record/field renames are part of the reader schema, so a producer rename must be declared with "aliases" or resolution breaks - the tolerance does not extend to renamed fields.

Avro's defaults never apply to values that are present (including nulls), and schema-registry compatibility checks must still be configured (BACKWARD/FORWARD/FULL) or a bad producer deploy will silently break readers.
